definition: Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011, the EU law that fixes permitted textile fiber names and requires fiber-composition labeling or marking of textile products placed on the EU market.
explanation: Adopted on 27 September 2011 and applicable from 8 May 2012, the Regulation replaced earlier directives with a single instrument that applies directly in every member state. Only the names listed in its Annex I may be used to describe fiber composition, and trade names cannot stand in for them. Products must carry a label or marking giving the full fiber composition in those names, and the Regulation adds rules on multi-fiber products, tolerances and the declaration of non-textile parts of animal origin. Further annexes set out methods for quantitative analysis of fiber mixtures, and the Commission can amend the annexes by delegated act.
example: An EU retailer sources a jacket shell that its supplier calls 'high-performance eco-nylon.' For the composition label, that description has to be translated into Annex I vocabulary, which offers 'polyamide or nylon' for this polymer class, with a percentage. A good exercise is to rewrite several supplier descriptions into Annex I names and notice how much promotional language falls away once only the regulated names remain.
caution: The Regulation governs fiber names and composition, not environmental claims, origin or care symbols. Words such as 'organic' or 'recycled' are not Annex I fiber names; claims of that kind fall under other EU and national rules, including the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive as amended by Directive (EU) 2024/825. Labels must also be provided in the official language or languages of the member state where the product is sold.
deeper: Annex I is a numbered table pairing each name with a description of the fiber, using compositional definitions for manufactured polymers that follow an approach similar to ISO 2076. Natural names include wool, silk, cotton and flax (or linen); manufactured names include viscose, modal, lyocell, cupro, polyester, 'polyamide or nylon' and elastane. A producer seeking a new name submits a technical file to the Commission, and a delegated act can then add it; Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/122 is one amendment that updated Annex I. For verification, the analysis annexes rely mainly on selective dissolution: a reagent dissolves one component, the residue is dried and weighed, and a correction factor compensates for slight mass loss of the undissolved fiber.
origins: Before 2011, EU textile naming rested on directives that each member state had to transpose into national law, most recently Directive 2008/121/EC on textile names, alongside Directives 73/44/EEC and 96/73/EC on methods for analyzing fiber mixtures. Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 repealed all three and, by using a regulation instead of a directive, made one text directly applicable across the Union and gave a faster route for adding names for new fibers.

definition: Fabric weight is mass per unit area, usually stated in grams per square meter (GSM, g/m2) or ounces per square yard, and sometimes misleadingly as ounces per linear yard.
explanation: Mass per unit area summarizes how much material a fabric contains, which correlates with properties such as opacity, warmth and durability but does not determine them. Standard methods cut specimens of known area from conditioned fabric and weigh them, or weigh full pieces of measured length and width. The figure depends on everything upstream: fiber density, yarn count, thread density, knit loop length and finishing shrinkage. Some sectors, notably denim, historically quote ounces per linear yard at the fabric's own width, which is not comparable across different widths.
example: A catalog lists one T-shirt jersey at 200 g/m2 and another at 5.9 oz/yd2. These are essentially the same weight, since 5.9 multiplied by 33.906 is about 200. A denim sold as 12 oz per linear yard at 58 inches wide is a different case: dividing by the width and multiplying by 36 gives about 7.4 oz/yd2, or roughly 253 g/m2.
caution: Weight is not quality, thickness or warmth by itself. A lofty knit and a dense woven can share a GSM yet feel and perform very differently. Finished weight also shifts with moisture, washing shrinkage and finishing, so compare conditioned values measured by the same method. Always ask whether an ounce figure is per square yard or per linear yard.
deeper: Mass per unit area equals specimen mass divided by specimen area after conditioning in a standard atmosphere, since fibers such as cotton and wool absorb moisture and gain mass. The unit conversion follows from 1 ounce being 28.35 grams and 1 square yard being 0.8361 square meters: 1 oz/yd2 is about 33.906 g/m2, the factor used in ASTM D3776/D3776M. Converting ounces per linear yard requires the width: oz/yd2 equals oz per linear yard divided by width in inches, multiplied by 36. ISO 3801 treats woven fabrics and distinguishes mass per unit length from mass per unit area, noting that for some structures these are not related simply by width. For a woven, areal mass can be estimated from ends and picks per centimeter, yarn tex values and crimp allowances.
origins: Weighing cloth by the piece or by the running yard is long-standing trade practice because fabric was sold off the roll. International and national standards later fixed how to condition, sample and calculate: ISO 3801 for woven fabrics dates from 1977, and ASTM D3776 covers mass per unit area of fabric in both inch-pound and SI units. The metric GSM figure has since become the common language of international sourcing.
